    Personal Guidance
    Balarāma, learning Kṛṣṇa has gone alone to steal the bride and fearing fight, hurries to Kuṇḍina with a mighty army. The elder brother's love reads the situation correctly and brings backup; family solidarity is muscular.
    Reflection Questions
    • Whose 'Balarāma' could you call to back up a risky mission?
    • Where do you go alone when an elder's army would serve the outcome better?
    Analogy

    An elder brother saddles his horse the moment he hears his younger brother has ridden out alone. Balarāma's anxiety is not doubt; it is the protective vātsalya of agraja-bhakti — Bhagavān's own brother loves Him as a brother loves.

    Stories
    Lakṣmaṇa following Rāma into the forest

    When Rāma was exiled, Lakṣmaṇa packed his bow and arrows without consulting anyone — kingdom, mother, wife all left behind. He could not bear that Rāma should be without him for a single night.

    Gauḍīyas read Balarāma's race to Kuṇḍina in this same light: agraja-sneha. Where the younger has gone, the elder follows with an army, because love does not separate well from worry.

    Important Words
    • kāṅkṣantī — waiting for
      Present participle of √kāṅkṣ (to long for). The same root behind ākāṅkṣā, longing — Rūpa Gosvāmī's term for the seed of bhāva. Rukmiṇī's longing is described in the same grammar Gauḍīyas use for the highest devotional desire.
    • āgamanam hareḥ — the arrival of Kṛṣṇa
      Accusative + genitive. The first time in this chapter Kṛṣṇa is named Hari — 'the one who steals.' Vyāsa is queuing the rasa: the bride waits for Hari, and Hari is on His way to live up to His name.
    • acintayat — she thought
      Imperfect of √cint. The internal monologue that follows (verses 23–26) is one of the great proto-prayer passages of the Bhāgavatam. Gauḍīyas treat this thinking as antaraṅga-cintana — the inner movement of the devotee toward Bhagavān.
    The lovely daughter of Bhīṣmaka anxiously awaited the arrival of Kṛṣṇa, but when she did not see the brāhmaṇa return she thought as follows.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    The lovely daughter of Bhīṣmaka anxiously awaited the arrival of Kṛṣṇa, but when she did not see the brāhmaṇa return she thought as follows.
    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Five and a half verses describe again the pūrva-rāga of Rukmiṇī in order to show the rasa of fresh association. The present verse shows her good fortune of having proper inner impressions. She was the best of whose who had attained the highest state of greed for Kṛṣṇa as a husband (varārohā). This is Śukadeva’s intention in using the word. Or the phrase can mean “she who had the best hips.” This reveals her age, and thus her suitability to have intense feelings of love. She constantly desired the coming of Kṛṣṇa who stole her mind and would take her away (hareḥ). Not seeing the brāhmaṇa return with news about him, she began to think.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    After describing Kṛṣṇa’s preparations for abducting her, five and a half verses describe Rukmiṇī’s bhāva. She had the best hips. This indicates her great beauty. She constantly desired the coming of Kṛṣṇa who stole her mind and would take her away (hareḥ). Not seeing the return of the messenger who would speak of Kṛṣṇa coming, she began to worry in the early morning (tadā). Being the daughter of Bhīṣkama, she was anxious that Kṛṣṇa come and abduct her.

    Personal Guidance
    The lovely daughter of Bhīṣmaka anxiously awaits Kṛṣṇa's arrival, but seeing the brāhmaṇa hasn't returned, she thinks. Waiting before an event becomes its own dense interior; the mind narrates the gap.
    Reflection Questions
    • What anxious interior do you generate in the gap before promised arrivals?
    • How could you steady that interior without canceling the genuine concern?
    Analogy

    A woman at the threshold of dawn watching the road — every sound is hooves, every silence a betrayal. Rukmiṇī's wait names the bhakta's classic posture: ākāṅkṣā, longing that has no other employment, looking for the one Person who has been promised.

    Stories
    The gopīs at the rāsa-sthala

    When Kṛṣṇa withdrew Himself in the middle of the rāsa-līlā, the gopīs searched the forest, asked the trees, the creepers, the deer — every leaf interrogated. SB 10.30 is one long verse of waiting.

    The Gauḍīyas read Rukmiṇī's wait here as a Dvārakā-side echo: the same longing wears different rasa-clothes. Vaidarbhī as the bride waiting; the gopīs as the lovers waiting — but the heart is one.

    Important Words
    • tri - yāma — three yāmas (the night)
      Compound: tri (three) + yāma (a three-hour watch). The Sanskrit night is three yāmas of three hours each; Rukmiṇī is counting them. Gauḍīya texts on smaraṇa-sādhana use the same yāma-divisions to organize aṣṭa-kāla bhajana.
    • alpa - rādhasaḥ — whose good fortune is insufficient
      Compound: alpa (little) + rādhas (gift, success, also a root playfully near 'Rādhā'). The bride laments her 'small rādhas.' Caitanya-caritāmṛta-style commentators savor that Rukmiṇī's fortune is small only because she is not yet visibly with Hari — the fortune itself is on its way.
    • aravinda - akṣaḥ — the lotus-eyed
      Compound: aravinda (lotus) + akṣa (eye). One of Kṛṣṇa's standard epithets in the SB. Rukmiṇī's calling Him by His beauty-name even in her lament shows her bhāva: even in viraha she names what she loves about Him.
    [Princess Rukmiṇī thought:] Alas, my wedding is to take place when the night ends! How unlucky I am! Lotus-eyed Kṛṣṇa does not come. I don’t know why. And even the brāhmaṇa messenger has not yet returned.
    Purport

    It is apparent from this verse, as confirmed by Śrīla Śrīdhara Svāmī, that the present scene takes place before sunrise.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    [Princess Rukmiṇī thought:] Alas, my wedding is to take place when the night ends! How unlucky I am! Lotus-eyed Kṛṣṇa does not come. I don't know why. And even the brāhmaṇa messenger has not yet returned.
    Commentary

    Before the sunrise, because of eagerness and fear, Rukmini began to worry. "This night of three yamas has finished. Tomorrow night is the fixed time for the wedding of this most unfortunate woman."

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Oh (aho)! She laments. Tri-yāma (nine hours) indicates a small amount of time. It is my bad luck Kṛṣṇa has not come, that I have not met him. There can be no other cause than my misfortune since he has all powers and protects those who surrender to him. That is also the cause of the brāhmaṇa not returning. If the merciful brāhmaṇa does not return, I will have to give up my life.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Oh (aho)! She laments. She is most unfortunate because Kṛṣṇa delays in coming. He does not come. The present tense is used to express the past to indicate that he must come. His lotus eyes destroy all suffering. I do not understand the reason why he has not come since he is endowed with all powers and he is affectionate to his devotees. Because he is completely independent, he will not come. Why would the brāhmaṇa return?

    Personal Guidance
    Alas, my wedding is at night's end! Unlucky me — lotus-eyed Kṛṣṇa doesn't come, and the brāhmaṇa hasn't returned. The bride names her circumstances; honest naming of perceived bad luck is permitted in scripture.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where do you suppress 'alas' when scripture grants it as legitimate speech?
    • How does naming unluckiness coexist with continued faith?
    Analogy

    A lamp lit before dawn, watching the wick gutter, hearing footsteps that never come. Rukmiṇī counts the yāmas — the night-watches of the bhakta's prayer, the calendar of separation. Vipralambha is bhakti's higher rasa precisely because absence sharpens the heart.

      Compound: an + avadya (faultless) + ātmā (self, body). The same anavadya-word the verse 3 applied to Rukmiṇī's body. Vyāsa is pairing them: faultless Lord, faultless bride; the only flaw is in Rukmiṇī's anxious imagination.
    • jugupsitam — contemptible
      From √gup (desiderative). The strongest aesthetic-moral word for repugnance. Rukmiṇī imagines Kṛṣṇa might have found her jugupsita — the most charged self-doubt a bhakta can voice. Gauḍīyas read the line as kārpaṇya (the sixth limb of śaraṇāgati): the devotee's humble self-estimate.
    • pāṇi - grahaṇe — for the taking of the hand
      Compound: pāṇi (hand) + grahaṇa (taking). The technical term for the wedding hand-clasp. Rukmiṇī uses the formal term — she is thinking of marriage in śāstric vocabulary even while emotionally collapsing.
    Perhaps the faultless Lord, even while preparing to come here, saw something contemptible in me and therefore has not come to take my hand.
    Purport

    Princess Rukmiṇī boldly invited Śrī Kṛṣṇa to kidnap her. When Rukmiṇī did not see Him come, she naturally feared that He had rejected her proposal, perhaps finding some unacceptable quality in her. As expressed here, the Lord Himself is anavadya, faultless, and if He saw some fault in Rukmiṇī she would be an unworthy bride for Him. It was natural for the young princess to feel such anxiety. Furthermore, if Śrī Kṛṣṇa had actually made this decision, it would be natural for the brāhmaṇa to fear Rukmiṇī’s reaction were he to bring her the news, and that would explain why he had not come.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Perhaps the faultless Lord, even while preparing to come here, saw something contemptible in me and therefore has not come to take my hand.
    Commentary

    She expresses doubt with the word "api". At first he was ready to come, and therefore because he would bring the brahmana with him, did not send the brahmana first. However at the time of leaving, seeing some fault n my body or intelligence, he gave up his plan. It would be improper for him, who is faultless in body and mind (anavadyatma) to marry me who am full of faults. And the brahmana being unsuccessful, has not come, fearing that I would give up my body.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    In great pain, she imagines another reason for the Lord and the brāhmaṇa not coming. Perhaps (nūnam) he has not come because, though he is without faults like hard-heartedness, he has seen something faulty in me. Because he is merciful he started to come, but then did not. Or, according to Hari-vaṁśa, after hearing of Rukmiṇī’s choice of a husband, Kṛṣṇa thought of leaving Mathurā for Kuṇḍina, where Indra had previously performed a ceremony enthroning Kṛṣṇa while Śiśupāla and others fled. The brāhmaṇa was delayed because Kṛṣṇa delayed.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    In great pain, she imagines another reason for the Lord and the brāhmaṇa not coming. The Lord has a most beautiful body, or is faultless in character. For certain (nūnam) he will not come to take my hand, though he made effort to come here (api). Or perhaps (nūnam), though he is without faults like hard-heartedness, he has seen something faulty in me because (hi) he has not come. Thus the brāhmaṇa wants to die (kṛtodyamaḥ). It is not stated directly since it is inauspicious.

    Personal Guidance
    Perhaps the faultless Lord saw something contemptible in me and therefore won't come to take my hand. Self-doubt under delay invents reasons He has lost interest; the heart looks for the failure inside itself.
    Reflection Questions
    • What 'contemptible something' do you imagine Kṛṣṇa has seen in you under delay?
    • Could compassion for that self-judgment loosen its grip?
    Analogy

    A devotee fears the Lord has seen something unworthy in her and turned away. The fear is groundless, but it is precisely the fear that proves the bhakti — only one who values Bhagavān can dread being unworthy of Him. Self-doubt at this register is itself a symptom of love.

    Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam 10.53.25

    Important Words
    • dhātā — the creator (Lord Brahmā)
      Nominative of dhātṛ (placer, arranger). Brahmā as the maker of destinies. Rukmiṇī blames the secondary creator rather than the supreme Person — Gauḍīyas treat this as theologically precise: karma's arranger may seem to fail, but Bhagavān never does.
    • mahā - īśvaraḥ — the great Lord Śiva
      Compound: mahā (great) + īśvara (controller). Śiva is great, but in Gauḍīya theology śivaḥ śakti-yutaḥ — controller of his śakti, and a Vaiṣṇava himself (vaiṣṇavānāṁ yathā śambhuḥ). Rukmiṇī's invoking him here is structurally correct: she is heading to Ambikā's temple in the next scene.
    • gaurī rudrāṇī giri - jā satī — Gaurī, the wife of Rudra, daughter of the mountain, Satī
      Four names of Pārvatī. Vyāsa stacks them to show that Rukmiṇī is in a fully traditional, Smārta cosmology — and yet her real prayer (verse 46) will ask Ambikā only to give her Kṛṣṇa. The Gauḍīya frame: even devī-pūjā culminates in Vaiṣṇava aspiration.
    I am extremely unfortunate, for the creator is not favorably disposed toward me, nor is the great Lord Śiva. Or perhaps Śiva’s wife, Devī, who is known as Gaurī, Rudrāṇī, Girijā and Satī, has turned against me.
    Purport

    Śrīla Viśvanātha Cakravartī explains that Rukmiṇī might have thought, “Even if Kṛṣṇa wanted to come, He might have been stopped on the path by the creator, Brahmā, who is not favorably inclined toward me. But why should he be unfavorable? Perhaps it is Maheśvara, Lord Śiva, whom on some occasion I did not properly worship and who thus became angry with me. But he is Maheśvara, the great controller, so why would he be angry with such an insignificant and foolish girl as me? “Perhaps it is Śiva’s wife, Gaurīdevī, who is displeased, though I worship her every day. Alas, alas, how have I offended her so that she has turned against me? But after all, she is Rudrāṇī, the wife of Rudra, and her very name means ‘one who makes everyone cry.’ So perhaps she and Śiva want me to cry. But seeing that I am so miserable, about to give up my life, why don’t they soften their attitude? The reason must be that Goddess Devī is Girijā, an adopted daughter, so why should she be soft-hearted? In her incarnation as Satī she gave up her body, so perhaps she now wants me to give up my body also.” Thus the ācārya, with realized poetic sensitivity, interprets the various names used in this verse.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    I am extremely unfortunate, for the creator is not favorably disposed toward me, nor is the great Lord Śiva. Or perhaps Śiva's wife, Devī, who is known as Gaurī, Rudrāṇī, Girijā and Satī, has turned against me.
    Commentary

    In this verse Rukmini speaks with great anxiety again. The creator is not favorable to me, for he has created some obstacle on Krsna’s path. Why he is displeased with me I cannot understand. Siva is angered perhaps by not receiving my worship sometime. But since his full of such great powers, he would not become angry with an insignificant girl like me. Though I worship her daily, Durga devi has rejected me. What offense have I done to her that she would reject me? Is this perhaps her very nature? She is the wife of Rudra (Rudrani). Rudra makes people cry. So perhaps she too is making me cry. Seeing my suffering, even to the extent that I will give up my life, why does her heart not melt? There must some fault in her heritage. Being the daughter of a mountain (girija), how could her heart melt, being so stone-like? She will make me give up my body I am certain, just as she gave up her body in her previous life (Sati).

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    She thinks of another cause of her misfortune, not considering that the faultless Lord sees faults in her. Though I have worshipped Brahmā and Śiva, they do not favor me. But one should receive good fortune from worshipping Brahmā and Śiva. She then thinks of another reason. Though Durgā is our family deity, she does not favor me since I have not worshipped her properly. Because she is so indifferent, Brahmā and Śiva are also unfavorable to me. She thinks of another cause, since Durgā is dependent on her husband. Though dependent on Śiva (rudrāṇi), she was born again (girijāḥ). First she was born as Satī, the daughter of Dakṣa, and later as Girijā, from the Himalayas. Hearing her husband was insulted, she gave up her life. It is suitable that I give up my life on not attaining Kṛṣṇa. Another version has giriśa: one who did austerities of sleeping on a mountain. She then began weeping profusely. This is understood from the next verse.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    I am most unfortunate because the Lord and Śiva do not favor me. They have the power to remove obstacles. Devī is our family deity. She is golden but previously was black. By undergoing great austerities, she became golden. She is fully devoted to Śiva. Or as Rudrāṇī she is pure, devoid of faults like hardness. She knows the pain that a girl undergoes to obtain a husband. She had two births. She was born from the mountain (girijā). Another version has girīśā. Being similar to Śiva, she is affectionate to the devotees. As Satī she has all good qualities. She cried profusely since later it is said aśru-kalākule.

    Personal Guidance
    I am unfortunate; the creator is not favorably disposed, nor Śiva — or perhaps Devī (Gaurī, Rudrāṇī, Girijā, Satī) has turned against me. Self-blame escalates to cosmic conspiracy; the heart looks for any explanation but reality.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where does your anxiety escalate from local to cosmic-conspiracy framing?
    • How do you catch yourself before that escalation finishes?
    Analogy

    A girl casting about for any cause of her abandonment names Brahmā, Śiva, Gaurī — anyone except Kṛṣṇa Himself. Even in fear, she cannot accuse the Lord; she would rather invent enemies among the highest devas. This is bhakti's reflex: protect Bhagavān from blame even at one's own expense.

    Stories
    Sītā in the Aśoka-vana

    Imprisoned by Rāvaṇa, Sītā never imagined Rāma had abandoned her — she searched only for what fault in herself had earned the separation. Vālmīki repeats: she would die rather than blame her Lord.

    Gauḍīyas pair SB 10.53.25 with this attitude. Rukmiṇī's accusing the demigods rather than Kṛṣṇa is the same śuddha-bhāva: better the universe be against me than that He should be.

    Important Words
    • govinda - hṛta - mānasā — whose mind was stolen by Kṛṣṇa
      Compound: Govinda + hṛta (stolen) + mānasā (mind). The Gauḍīya tradition glosses Govinda as 'the one who gives pleasure to the cows and the senses.' Rukmiṇī's mind is hṛta — He has stolen it before He steals her body, a typical kāvya inversion.
    • kāla - jñā — knowing the time
      Compound: kāla (time) + jñā (knower). Rukmiṇī knows the muhūrta will not pass for several more hours. Gauḍīyas note: even in distress she keeps śāstric awareness — bhakti does not destroy intelligence, it sharpens it.
    • aśru - kalā - ākule — brimming with tears
      Compound: aśru (tear) + kalā (small portion, fragment) + ākula (filled). Tears are an aṣṭa-sāttvika-bhāva sign in Rūpa Gosvāmī's Bhakti-rasāmṛta-sindhu. The poet is using the technical vocabulary of rasa-śāstra.
    As she thought in this way, the young maiden, whose mind had been stolen by Kṛṣṇa, closed her tear-filled eyes, remembering that there was still time.
    Purport

    Śrīla Śrīdhara Svāmī explains the word kāla-jñā as follows: “[Rukmiṇī thought,] ‘It is not even the right time yet for Govinda to come,’ and thus she felt a bit consoled.”

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    As she thought in this way, the young maiden, whose mind had been stolen by Kṛṣṇa, closed her tear-filled eyes, remembering that there was still time.
    Commentary

    "O fickle mind! Do not prepare to give up your body now, because the time of his coming has not yet passed. Before giving up the body, let me see his face in meditation one time. You should not prevent this, dear mind." Then she closed her eyes.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Her mind had been stolen by Kṛṣṇa, who was the lord of the cows, having the sweetness of Gokula. Though a young girl, she began thinking in this way. In grief she did not think of anything else. Her eyes were filled with tear drops or were agitated with tear drops. Another version has jalākule. She was aware that Govinda had not come even now (kāla-jṣāḥ), when the procession was about to begin.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Her mind was absorbed in Kṛṣṇa, the lord who appeared on earth to display his unlimited powers (govinda). Though she was a young girl (bālāḥ) she thought in this way only, full of lamentation. Her eyes were full of drops of tears or a torrent of tears. She closed her eyes to stop the tears from falling because of great pain. Or though she knew there was still time, she closed her eyes in great pain. This means she fainted. Or desiring to close her eyes, she desired to die. It is later mentioned: dūtas tvayātma-labhane su-vivikta-mantraḥ prasthāpito mayi cirāyati śūnyam etat matvā jihāsa idaṁ aṅgam ananya-yogyaṁ tiṣṭheta tat tvayi vayaṁ pratinandayāmaḥ When you sent the messenger with your most confidential plan and yet I delayed going to you, you began to see the whole world as void and wanted to quit your body, which could never have been given to anyone but me. May this greatness of yours remain with you always; I can do nothing to reciprocate except joyfully thank you for your devotion. SB 10.60.57

    Personal Guidance
    Mind stolen by Kṛṣṇa, the young maiden closes her tear-filled eyes, remembering there is still time. Even in despair, scripture restores time-awareness; the right hour is still pending.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where do you forget that 'there is still time' under emotional pressure?
    • What small remembrance restores the right sense of timing?
    Analogy

    A lover closes her eyes not to sleep but to see better — the inner Kṛṣṇa is more real than the empty road outside. Gauḍīyas call this dhyāna in the mood of vipralambha: the eyes close, the heart opens.

    Important Words
    • vāmaḥ ūruḥ bhujaḥ netram — left thigh, arm, and eye
      Three body parts. In nimitta-śāstra, twitching of the left limbs is auspicious for a woman, the right for a man. Vyāsa records the precise omen-grammar; Gauḍīyas note that even sub-rational signals of the body are precise instruments of Bhagavān's communication.
    • asphuran — twitched
      Imperfect of √sphur (to throb, quiver). Same root as sphūrti — the sudden spiritual experience Gauḍīyas describe in advanced sādhana. Rukmiṇī experiences a bodily sphūrti foreshadowing Kṛṣṇa's appearance.
    • priya - bhāṣiṇaḥ — speaking something desirable
      Compound: priya (dear, desirable) + bhāṣin (speaker). The omens 'speak' priya — the same word that names the Beloved in rasa-śāstra. The body whispers the name of the One coming.
    O King, as the bride thus awaited the arrival of Govinda, she felt a twitch in her left thigh, arm and eye. This was a sign that something desirable would happen.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    O King, as the bride thus awaited the arrival of Govinda, she felt a twitch in her left thigh, arm and eye. This was a sign that something desirable would happen.
    Commentary

    Her left thigh and other bodily limbs began to tremble. This was a sign of auspiciousness.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Rukmiṇī, whose marriage was approaching (vadhvaḥ), was awaiting the arrival of Kṛṣṇa. Her left, thigh, arm and eye twitched. The limbs are mentioned from lower to higher in placement, but they simultaneously began to quiver. The verb is the subject of each noun. Priya-bhāsinaḥ should be in the neuter to agree with netram, but is in the masculine as poetic license.

    Personal Guidance
    As the bride awaits Govinda, she feels a twitch in her left thigh, arm, and eye — a sign that something desirable will happen. Devotees read bodily signs; small twitches can be authentic premonition.
    Reflection Questions
    • What small subtle signs in your body have you been ignoring as possible auspicious indicators?
    • How could you honor the body's pre-cognitions without superstition?
    Analogy

    The body of the devotee becomes a small prophet, twitching at the approach of Bhagavān before the mind has noticed. Auspicious omens are not superstition in śāstra; they are the registration of Kṛṣṇa's nearness in flesh that does not yet know how to speak.

    Important Words
    • kṛṣṇa - vinirdiṣṭaḥ — ordered by Lord Kṛṣṇa
      Compound: Kṛṣṇa + vinirdiṣṭa (specifically directed). The brāhmaṇa moves under Bhagavān's direct instruction. Gauḍīyas treat his role as paramparā in miniature: a brāhmaṇa carries Kṛṣṇa's word to the awaiting devotee.
    • dvija - sat - tamaḥ — the most pure of brāhmaṇas
      Compound: dvija (twice-born) + sat (true, real) + tama (superlative). Vyāsa rates the messenger at the top of brāhmaṇa-quality. The Gauḍīya signature: bhakti's intermediaries are themselves saintly, never mere couriers.
    • devīm — the goddess, Rukmiṇī
      Accusative of devī. The Bhāgavata calls Rukmiṇī devī because she is Lakṣmī Herself. Gauḍīyas insist that the bride here is not a mortal princess being elevated; she is the eternal consort of Bhagavān taking the līlā-form.
    Just then the purest of learned brāhmaṇas, following Kṛṣṇa’s order, came to see the divine Princess Rukmiṇī within the inner chambers of the palace.
    Purport

    According to Śrīla Śrīdhara Svāmī, Śrī Kṛṣṇa had reached the gardens outside the city, and out of concern for Rukmiṇī He had instructed the brāhmaṇa to tell her of His arrival.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Just then the purest of learned brāhmaṇas, following Kṛṣṇa's order, came to see the divine Princess Rukmiṇī within the inner chambers of the palace.
    Commentary

    The brahmana was instructed particularly (vi nirdistah), by Krsna, "Tell her that I have come to a garden in the city." He saw Rukmini, who was radiant (devi) due to bliss, having seen Krsna in meditation. She was about to leave her chambers to come to Krsna influenced by her meditation.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The brāhmaṇa had been ordered by Kṛṣṇa, and no one else, since he was qualified. “Tell her that she has attained me. I will take her away.” First he saw her. She did not see him first, because she was moving about here and there with restless heart within the palace to see if the brāhmaṇa had come. She was shining with the ornaments for marriage (devīm). Ha indicates joy. He was wondering while coming whether he would be able to see Rukmiṇī or not, since Rukmī was so devious. Therefore he was joyous when he saw her.

    Personal Guidance
    Just then the purest learned brāhmaṇa, by Kṛṣṇa's order, comes to see Rukmiṇī in the inner chambers. The messenger arrives exactly when the heart can bear no more; timing of grace meets the threshold of despair.
    Reflection Questions
    • When has a messenger arrived exactly as you couldn't bear more?
    • What gratitude could you offer for grace arriving at the limit?
    Analogy

    A messenger walks back through the same gates he left, this time carrying not a question but an answer. The brāhmaṇa's return is the structural turn of the chapter: Rukmiṇī's prayer has been heard.

    Important Words
    • lakṣaṇa - abhijñā — expert knower of symptoms
      Compound: lakṣaṇa (sign) + abhijñā (knowing well). Rukmiṇī reads signs the way a śāstra-jña reads texts. Gauḍīyas read lakṣaṇa-jñāna as a bhakti-virtue: the devotee perceives Bhagavān's signals everywhere.
    • prahṛṣṭa - vadanam — whose face was filled with joy
      Compound: pra-hṛṣṭa (very joyful) + vadana (face). The hṛṣṭa-state is one of Rūpa's anubhāvas. The brāhmaṇa's face itself broadcasts the good news; Rukmiṇī need not even hear the words yet.
    • śuci - smitā — with a pure smile
      Compound: śuci (pure) + smitā (smiling). The same śuci-smita epithet recurs for Rukmiṇī in 53.51–55. Gauḍīyas link it to viśuddha-sattva — the bhāva-bhakta's smile is unmixed with worldly motive.
    Noting the brāhmaṇa’s joyful face and serene movements, saintly Rukmiṇī, who could expertly interpret such symptoms, inquired from him with a pure smile.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Noting the brāhmaṇa's joyful face and serene movements, saintly Rukmiṇī, who could expertly interpret such symptoms, inquired from him with a pure smile.
    Commentary

    "I, Sunanda brahmana, have come now from you beloved. Please cast your glance upon me,." said the brahmana in a loud voice. Rukmini, her meditation broken, then say him standing there. Because the brahmana’s mind was not disturbed he was smiling broadly. Seeing that, Rukmini ‘s anxiety disappeared, because she was knowledgeable of omens indicating success—the joy in the brahmana’s eyes and smile, and the quivering of the left side of her body. She them smiled slightly, indicating her genuine (suci) joy. Previously she had been falsely smiling, to hide her inner suffering.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    She smiled out of joy since she knew the symptoms of good news, since she was endowed to the highest degree with all good qualities (satī). She questioned him completely with respect, asking how he was etc. She asked the brāhmaṇa who was moving serenely with joyous face. Or she, with serenity (avyagrā), asked him thoroughly about Kṛṣṇa who was her shelter (ātma-gatim). Where is he? What did he say?

    Personal Guidance
    Noting the brāhmaṇa's joyful face and serene movements, saintly Rukmiṇī — expert in such symptoms — inquires with a pure smile. Reading the messenger's face is part of devotional intelligence; symptoms precede words.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where do you wait for words when faces already report?
    • What 'symptom-reading' could improve your reception of messengers in your life?
    Analogy

    A devotee reads the master's face before any words are spoken — every gesture is scripture if you have learned the alphabet. Rukmiṇī is lakṣaṇa-abhijñā, a literate reader of bodily signs; her bhakti has trained her to interpret the smallest gesture as news of Kṛṣṇa.

    Important Words
    • satya - vacanam — words of assurance / true word
      Compound: satya (truth) + vacana (speech). One of Bhagavān's six opulences in Gauḍīya theology — He is sva-bhāvataḥ satya-saṅkalpa, His vow is the fact. Caitanya-caritāmṛta cites this property as a sign of Bhagavattā.
    • ātma - upanayanam — His marriage with her (literally: bringing her near to Himself)
      Compound: ātma (self) + upanayana (leading near). The same word as the upanayana-saṁskāra, where the brāhmaṇa-child is led to the guru. Gauḍīyas note the resonance: marriage to Kṛṣṇa is being led near to the ātmā of all selves.
    • yadu - nandanam — Kṛṣṇa, the child of the Yadus
      Compound: Yadu + nandana (delighter, child). Echoes verse 1. The brāhmaṇa names Him by His dynastic-sweet name — bringing Rukmiṇī into the family that Kṛṣṇa has chosen to inhabit.
    The brāhmaṇa announced to her the arrival of Lord Yadunandana and relayed the Lord’s promise to marry her.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    The brāhmaṇa announced to her the arrival of Lord Yadunandana and relayed the Lord's promise to marry her.
    Commentary

    He described to her his meeting with Krsna. He described how Krsna had promised to come to her, relating his words such as "I will bring Rukmini." (sb 10.153.3)

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    He announced that he had met Kṛṣṇa, who gives joy to the Yadus (yadu-nandanam). Rukmiṇī praised him. Or, the brāhmaṇa announced he had met Kṛṣṇa, that Kṛṣṇa had come and what he said, and praised (śaśamṣa) Kṛṣṇa. Or the brāhmaṇa described (śaśaṁsa) Kṛṣṇa, that he had come, and what he said.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Kṛṣṇa who gives joy to the Yadus indicates that all the Yadus also came. The Lord had promised (satya-vacanam) to take her. He announced what he said to (prati) Kṛṣṇa (yadu-nandanam) and his promise to take her close to him (upanayanam). .

    Personal Guidance
    The brāhmaṇa announces the Lord's arrival and relays His promise to marry her. The message is two-part: He is here; He will do what He said.
    Reflection Questions
    • What two-part message from the Lord do you need to hear today — He is here, He will keep His word?
    • Where could you trust both halves?
    Analogy

    A satya-vacana is an arrow already in flight — once Kṛṣṇa has promised, the marriage has in some sense already happened, even though the bride still stands inside the inner chamber. Bhagavān's word and Bhagavān's deed do not differ in time.

    Stories
    Prahlāda's pillar

    When Prahlāda said 'My Lord is everywhere, even in this pillar,' Hiraṇyakaśipu broke the pillar in mockery — and Nṛsiṁha emerged. The boy's word was Kṛṣṇa's deed.

    Gauḍīyas read 10.53.30 the same way: Kṛṣṇa's satya-vacana to marry Rukmiṇī is itself the marriage. The chariot ride is mere unfolding of a vow already enacted.

    Important Words
    • hṛṣṭa - mānasā — whose mind was gladdened
      Compound: hṛṣṭa (joyful) + mānasā (mind). The same hṛṣṭa-state as the brāhmaṇa's face in verse 29 — joy passing between devotees. Gauḍīyas treat saṅkīrtana-style ānanda-transmission as the same dynamic: bhakti is contagious.
    • nanāma — she bowed down
      Perfect of √nam. Vandanam is one of the nine limbs of bhakti (SB 7.5.23). When material offerings fail, the bodily prostration remains; the limb that costs nothing material is sufficient.
    • vaidarbhī — Rukmiṇī, the princess of Vidarbha
      Patronymic. The first time in this chapter she is named only by her place. Gauḍīya commentators read this as her stepping forward as a soon-to-be Lakṣmī — the daughter of one place, on the threshold of becoming the queen of another.
    Princess Vaidarbhī was overjoyed to learn of Kṛṣṇa’s arrival. Not finding anything at hand suitable to offer the brāhmaṇa, she simply bowed down to him.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Princess Vaidarbhī was overjoyed to learn of Kṛṣṇa's arrival. Not finding anything at hand suitable to offer the brāhmaṇa, she simply bowed down to him.
    Commentary

    Thinking of what to give the brahmana to satisfy him, she just offered her respects. Not seeing any other object worthy of giving (priya), she offered respects to at least show her gratitude. But then the house of the brahmana became filled with all sorts of treasures. This was a response of Mahalaksmi to show her gratitude.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Understanding with certainty (sam—ājṣāya) that he had come, in an excited mood, she did not see anything suitable to offer the brāhmaṇa. Using na paśyantī instead of apaśyantī is poetic license. Later she gave him many gifts. When she was in Dvārakā she possessed infinite wealth, and gave him infinite gifts. She did not offer respects previously because she forgot, due to her bliss. Or not seeing any suitable item to give to him to repay him for what she had received, she felt defeated and just offered respects.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    She knew of Kṛṣṇa’s arrival, confirming it by various signs (sam-ājṣāya). She who was directly Lakṁsī (sā), surrendered to Kṛṣṇa alone, who was born in a suitable place called Vidarbha, known from scriptures as the place where the wife of Kṛṣṇa would be born as the daughter of the king. She did not see anything suitable to offer to the brāhmaṇa. Or she did not see anything except her beloved to be attained. Or seeing that he was pleased without material objects (anyat) she did not bow down. Love is not accomplished simply by bowing down for the person who desires prema for Kṛṣṇa. The person offers prema. She (sā) was famous as capable of offering bhakti to the Lord. She was famous as dearest to the Lord. She appeared in Vidarbha to manifest her unlimited powers similar to Kṛṣṇa’s.

    Personal Guidance
    Overjoyed, Vaidarbhī, not finding anything suitable at hand to offer the brāhmaṇa, simply bows down. When you have nothing material to give in gratitude, body bowing is enough.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where do you delay gratitude because you have nothing material to offer?
    • Could a bow be the right offering in the moment?
    Analogy

    Empty-handed before the messenger of God, she bows — having nothing to give, she gives herself. Daṇḍavat-praṇāma is the bhakta's reserve currency: when offerings fail, the body itself becomes the offering.

    Stories
    Vidura's banana peels

    When Kṛṣṇa visited Vidura's house, Vidurāṇī was so absorbed she fed the Lord banana peels and threw the fruit away — and Kṛṣṇa ate the peels with delight. SB 10.86 records that bhāva, not the offering, is what reaches Bhagavān.

    Rukmiṇī here has even less to give the brāhmaṇa, so she gives praṇāma. Gauḍīyas read both episodes together: bhakti's deepest gift is the bowed head.

    to Balarāma and Kṛṣṇa
    samarhaṇaiḥ
    with abundant offerings .
    Important Words
    • rāma - kṛṣṇau — Balarāma and Kṛṣṇa
      Dual compound. The two brothers are named in dual throughout the chapter — Gauḍīyas treat this as the SB-side parallel of Nityānanda-Caitanya: two Lords, one mission, the elder always present to amplify the younger.
    • samarhaṇaiḥ — with abundant offerings
      Instrumental plural of sam-arhaṇa (worship-offering). Bhīṣmaka uses the technical worship-vocabulary for what is socially a wedding-reception. Gauḍīyas read: when Bhagavān walks in, every greeting becomes pūjā whether the host knows or not.
    • udvāha - prekṣaṇa - utsukau — eager to witness the wedding
      Compound: udvāha (wedding) + prekṣaṇa (witnessing) + utsuka (eager). Kṛṣṇa pretends to be a wedding-guest. Gauḍīyas savor the līlā-irony: He has come to witness His own wedding — to a bride Bhīṣmaka thinks belongs to someone else.
    The King, upon hearing that Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma had come and were eager to witness his daughter’s wedding, went forth with abundant offerings to greet Them as music resounded.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    The King, upon hearing that Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma had come and were eager to witness his daughter's wedding, went forth with abundant offerings to greet Them as music resounded.
    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The king announced that the two had come for the wedding. It appeared that they had come like everyone else to see the wedding of his daughter to Śiśupāla. Thus Kṛṣṇa followed Rukmiṇī’s instructions and kept his motive secret, while being surrounded by his troops. The king felt very fortunate that the two had come to see the marriage of his (sva) daughter, though he was not qualified at all. Or he secretly felt that actually Kṛṣṇa should take her away. He worshipped them with the best items of worship (samarhanaiḥ).

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The king heard that the two had come into the city. They were eager to see the marriage directly. They were perceived to be coming to confirm the marriage of their maternal cousin. Thus Kṛṣṇa came first, alone. If he came with the Yadus, there would be worry that he came to steal the bride. He would arrange to have the bride protected. Rukmi and the army and would not allow her to go the temple. Thus, Rukmiṇī had instructed him to come secretly (verse 41). However they did not come for the wedding. He had come quickly out of great affection, with Balarāma, and both were welcomed by the king. According to the message, Kṛṣṇa should come first in secret, but he did not. Though he felt himself unqualified, the king felt himself fortunate that the two had come to see the wedding of his daughter. He was overjoyed that they came to see his (sva) daughter’s marriage. He felt internally that Kṛṣṇa should take her. Though Kṛṣṇa arrived first, Balarāma is mentioned first, since he was older. Bhīṣmaka worshipped them with the best items.

    Hearing Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma have come, the King goes forth with abundant offerings to greet Them as music resounds. Royal hospitality is multisensory; arrivals are met with offerings and music.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where do you welcome guests with less than full sensory hospitality?
    • What music could accompany your next welcome?
    Analogy

    Music meets music. The drums of the city sound for the false bridegroom even as the true Lord rides in to applause meant for another. Bhakti often arrives inside a celebration set up for something else; Bhagavān walks into the welcome and makes it His.

    Important Words
    • madhu - parkam — the traditional honey-milk mixture
      Compound: madhu (honey) + parka (mixture). The śāstric drink offered to a snātaka, king, ācārya, or bridegroom. Bhīṣmaka unknowingly performs the bridegroom-rite for Kṛṣṇa — the marriage has already begun ritually.
    • vidhi - vat — according to scriptural prescriptions
      Adverb: vidhi (rule) + suffix -vat. The same vidhi-vat that recurs throughout Bhīṣmaka's actions (verses 10, 16). Gauḍīyas note: rule-correct ritual offered to Bhagavān, even by accident, still reaches Him.
    • upāyanāni abhīṣṭāni — desirable presentations
      Compound: upāyana (gift) + abhīṣṭa (desired). The verb-root √iṣ (to wish) sits at the heart of abhīṣṭa. The gifts Bhīṣmaka thinks 'desirable' are in fact what Kṛṣṇa Himself desires — being received by His devotee's family.
    Presenting Them with madhu-parka, new clothing and other desirable gifts, he worshiped Them according to standard rituals.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Presenting Them with madhu-parka, new clothing and other desirable gifts, he worshiped Them according to standard rituals.
    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Having indicated the items, Śukadeva now describes how they were used. He brought the madhuparka near or offered it with service attitude as a gift. He also offered items dear to them or himself such as elephants, horses, and jewels. He worshipped them in a special way (sam) or as his son-in-laws.

    Important Words
    • śrī - mat — opulent
      Compound: śrī (splendor, Lakṣmī) + -mat (possessing). The accommodations are 'possessed of śrī' — and Rukmiṇī, who is Lakṣmī, is about to leave the city for these very accommodations. The word foreshadows.
    • ātithyam — hospitality
      From atithi (guest, literally 'one without a fixed time of arrival'). Atithi-sevā is one of the pañca-mahā-yajñas. Gauḍīyas note: hospitality to Bhagavān as guest is an eternal possibility — Caitanya-caritāmṛta describes Sārvabhauma similarly hosting Mahāprabhu.
    • mahā - matiḥ — generous (literally: of great mind)
      Compound: mahā (great) + mati (intelligence, mind). Bhīṣmaka is great-minded even if not great-discerning. Gauḍīyas distinguish mahā-mati (broad intelligence) from sumati (right intelligence); Bhīṣmaka has the former without the latter.
    Generous King Bhīṣmaka arranged opulent accommodations for the two Lords, and also for Their army and entourage. In this way he afforded Them proper hospitality.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Generous King Bhīṣmaka arranged opulent accommodations for the two Lords, and also for Their army and entourage. In this way he afforded Them proper hospitality.
    Commentary

    Bhismaka is described as generous (mahamatih) because he was contented in his heart, knowing that Krsna had come to marry his qualified daughter. Therefore he worshipped Krsna elaborately.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    With devotion he offered (upākalpya) them palaces with furnishings and enjoyments (śrīmat).

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    He offered accommodation with food, drinks, cloth, and ornaments (śrīmat) or with crystal pillars and unlimited beauty. He made special palaces for them and offered them as their servant or accepting them as his masters, or with all hospitality (sam). The followers were Gada, Satyaki, Uddhava and others. The four parts of the army were also there. He offered properly, with great devotion (yathā), with beds, water, food, milk products and butter.

    Important Words
    • yathā vīryam yathā vayaḥ yathā balam yathā vittam — according to power, age, strength, wealth
      Fourfold compound — the four mundane standards by which kṣatriya society ranks people. Gauḍīyas note: every one of these is irrelevant to Bhakti-rasāmṛta-sindhu's rankings, where only bhāva and rasa matter.
    • sametānām — who had assembled
      Genitive plural participle of sam-√i. The same kings who in verse 17 came to support Śiśupāla. Bhīṣmaka honors them like a good host; the next chapter will see them humiliated. Form and outcome diverge.
    • kāmaiḥ — with desirable things
      Instrumental plural of kāma. Material desirables, distinguished sharply in Gauḍīya literature from prema. Bhīṣmaka has only kāma to offer the kings; Kṛṣṇa will offer Rukmiṇī something else entirely.
    Thus it was that Bhīṣmaka gave all desirable things to the kings who had assembled for the occasion, honoring them as befitted their political power, age, physical prowess and wealth.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Thus it was that Bhīṣmaka gave all desirable things to the kings who had assembled for the occasion, honoring them as befitted their political power, age, physical prowess and wealth.
    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Vīryam means strength. Balam means armies. Sarva-kāmaiḥ means “with all enjoyments.”

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    He offered valuables to the kings who had gathered to see the wedding (evam), along with their armies or all together (sam-etānām) according to their strength (vīryam), their armies (balam). Those who had more power and armies received more goods. He worshipped all to satisfy their minds fully. In the list of strength, age, armies and wealth the former are greater causes for worship.

    Related values & verses
    Concepts
    Jiva
    Personal Guidance
    Bhīṣmaka gives desirable things to all assembled kings — honoring them according to power, age, prowess, wealth. Even when wrong, the host treats every guest with calibrated regard; standard differentiates correctly.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where do you flatten everyone equally when calibrated honoring would actually be just?
    • How do you measure and meet each guest in their actual scale?
    Analogy

    A host doles out honor in proportion to political weight — exactly the wrong scale for Bhagavān's company, who measures only bhakti. Bhīṣmaka's protocol is impeccable in this verse and irrelevant in the next: the actual hierarchy of Vidarbha is being rewritten by what is about to happen.

    Important Words
    • netra - añjalibhiḥ — with the cupped palms of their eyes
      Compound: netra (eye) + añjali (cupped palms). One of Vyāsa's signature kāvya-images. Gauḍīyas treat it as a model for darśana-bhakti: the eyes themselves become the offering-vessel.
    • papuḥ — they drank
      Perfect plural of √pā (to drink). The same verb the gopīs use for drinking Kṛṣṇa's flute-song (10.21.5). Vyāsa transplants the Vraja-vocabulary to Vidarbha — the citizens of Kuṇḍina momentarily become honorary gopīs.
    • mukha - paṅkajam — lotus face
      Compound: mukha (face) + paṅkaja (lotus). Kṛṣṇa's mukha-paṅkaja is the standard meditation-object for vaidhī-sādhana in Gauḍīya arcana-paddhati. The whole city is engaged in spontaneous unscripted dhyāna.
    When the residents of Vidarbha-pura heard that Lord Kṛṣṇa had come, they all went to see Him. With the cupped palms of their eyes they drank the honey of His lotus face.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    When the residents of Vidarbha-pura heard that Lord Kṛṣṇa had come, they all went to see Him. With the cupped palms of their eyes they drank the honey of His lotus face.
    Commentary

    The people drank the incomparable sweetness of Krsna’s lotus face. This indicates the quantity of sweetness of his face. It was wonderful because of the number of people drinking and the unlimited supply of sweetness of one face.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    They drank the honey of his face. This means the people tasted the intense sweetness of his beauty. Though the beauty and the face are different they are considered one in this verse (they drank his lotus face) because of intensity of the beauty. The metaphor of the cupped hands of their eyes suggests continuous drinking. It also suggests the drinkers had great thirst. What a marvelous lotus this was!

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The citizens of Vidarbha, men and women, heard that Kṛṣṇa, who attracts all hearts or who is the form of the highest bliss (bhagavān), had come. They gathered near him and drank the sweet beauty of his face, just as a bee drinks the nectar from the lotus out of attachment. They looked for a long time with absorption.

    Related values & verses
    Related values
    Bhakti (Devotion)Tejas (Inner Radiance / Vigour)Daksya (Resourcefulness / Skill)
    Related verses
    SB 1.2BG 14.1 BG 15.7 BG 15.9 BG 3.27 BG 3.3 BG 3.11 BG 9.11 BG 6.35 BG 14.12 BG 12.6 BG 15.2 BG 17.3 BG 5.4 BG 5.18 BG 12.5
    Concepts
    Jiva
    Personal Guidance
    When Vidarbha-pura's residents hear Kṛṣṇa has come, they go to see Him; with the cupped palms of their eyes they drink the honey of His lotus face. Spontaneous public response to the Lord uses bodily image — eyes as cupped palms drinking.
    Reflection Questions
    • When did you last 'drink' Kṛṣṇa with your eyes rather than just glance?
    • What changes when seeing becomes drinking?
    Analogy

    The whole city tilts forward at one news, drinking the Lord's face through their eyes as through cupped palms. Darśana in this verse is literally that — the eyes become añjali-mudrā, and the face of Kṛṣṇa becomes the water of the offering.

    Stories
    The women of Mathurā at Kṛṣṇa's arrival

    When Kṛṣṇa first entered Mathurā as a boy (SB 10.41), the women of the city ran to their windows and rooftops, drinking His form with their eyes — abandoning cooking, children, husbands. Vyāsa's image was unforgettable enough to be reused here in Vidarbha-pura.

    Gauḍīyas read both verses as the SB pattern: Bhagavān's bodily appearance does what no doctrine can — it pulls darśana through the eye like water through palms.

      Predicate noun + infinitive. The citizens are speaking in the language of marriage. Gauḍīyas note: Rukmiṇī as Lakṣmī is eternally bhāryā; the wedding is a temporal manifestation of an eternal fact.
    • anavadya - ātmā — whose bodily form is faultless
      Compound: an + avadya (faultless) + ātmā (body, self). The third occurrence of anavadya in this chapter (verses 3, 24, 37). Vyāsa keeps marking Kṛṣṇa and Rukmiṇī with the same word — they are anavadya for each other.
    • samucitaḥ patiḥ — most suitable husband
      Compound: samucita (fitting, suitable) + pati (husband, lord). Pati here is loaded — Gauḍīyas pun on its other meaning, Lord. Kṛṣṇa is samucita-pati not only as bridegroom but as Bhagavān, the only fitting Lord.
    [The people of the city said:] Rukmiṇī, and no one else, deserves to become His wife, and He also, possessing such flawless beauty, is the only suitable husband for Princess Bhaiṣmī.
    Purport

    According to Śrīla Viśvanātha Cakravartī, this text combines statements made by different citizens. Some pointed out that Rukmiṇī was a suitable wife for Kṛṣṇa, others said that no one else was suitable. Similarly, some stated that Kṛṣṇa was most suitable for Rukmiṇī, and others stated that no one else would be a suitable husband for her.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    [The people of the city said:] Rukmiṇī, and no one else, deserves to become His wife, and He also, possessing such flawless beauty, is the only suitable husband for Princess Bhaiṣmī.
    Commentary

    1. For him alone and no other. 2. As a wife not as an enjoyable object. 3. Rukmini alone and no one else. 4. This certainly must be, and should not be avoided. 5. He alone and no one else. 6. For Rukmini and no one else. 7. This must be done, without the slightest trace of doubt (samuchitah). These are the seven statements, with the negative qualifier "no one else nor nothing else" applied to each statement (napara). Because of the number of speakers there were numerous statements. Seven statements have been combined in one. Some said "Rukmini should be his wife and no one elses. Others said "She should be his wife and nothing else, such as object of enjoyment." Others said, "Rukmini alone, and no one else, should be his wife." In this way also four other statements could be made.(Rukmini should certainly be his wife, there is no question about it. Krsna and only Krsna should be Rukmini’s husband. Krsna should be the husband of Rukmini only. Krsna must be the husband of Rukmini.) To say it is a fault because of the impossibility of combining seven statements in one is not correct as there are authoritative statements which that it is possible to combine different statements in one.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    All were completely overcome on seeing the excellent suitability of Kṛṣṇa and Rukmiṇī. They speak in three verses. Kṛṣṇa alone (asya eva), and no one else, is suitable to be his wife and no one else except Rukmiṇī is suitable as his wife. He alone and no other is most suitable (samucitaḥ) as a husband for Rukmiṇī alone, and no one else. There is not even a little unsuitability in others. This is a different way of asserting the same fact. To derive another meaning from one statement is considered to be a fault since an imaginary meaning is not respected. One will not be able to obtain the true meaning if a statement has various interpretations. It is said śabda-buddhi-karmānāṁ viramya vyapārābhavah: when the function of words has been understood in a sentence their use is finished (a statement should be made only once). (This quoted in Sāhitya-darpaṇa commentary 1.23) However, the conclusion is stated in Śrīdhara Svāmī’s commentary. Anudya-vidheya-bhedena vibhinnānām eva vākyānām saha prayogāt: various statements can be used to express the same meaning in different words. Generally one should not repeat a statement. However one can do so eloquently by using different words. Thus Rukmiṇī should be the wife of Kṛṣṇa alone, not the wife of someone else. That is the first statement. Rukmiṇī alone should be the wife of Kṛṣṇa. That is the second statement. By use of the word eva (alone) the statements become different and thus fault is avoided, like cleaning a sacrificial spoon with a piece of cloth (grahaṁ samarṣṭi, a term from Pūrva-mīmāṁsa raised in Śrīdhara Svāmī’s commentary). The utensils become the main object, and also serve a purpose in the sacrificial rites. Thus all those particular items known as grahas should be purified, not just one. If the meaning is otherwise, the action becomes meaningless. In this particular instance the meaning of the sentence should be repeated so that all the vessels are cleansed, even though the statement is general. Similarly, statements may be repeated in a slightly different manner and this will not produce fault. The main object is expressed first by general indication and purpose. It is indicated by the particularizing, secondary word eva in this verse. In the first statement Rukmiṇī is stated to be most suitable as the wife of only Kṛṣṇa with Kṛṣṇa’s possessiveness as the intention and purpose. In the second statement only Rukmiṇī is suitable as the wife of Kṛṣṇa, with emphasis on Rukmiṇī. As in the case of cleaning the utensils, there is no fault in repetition of the statement in a different way. The word eva should be understood to with both asya and bhaiṣmyāḥ to indicate that they are mutually qualified in the same way. (He alone is qualified for her and she alone is qualified for him.) The word anavadyātmā (completely faultless) should also modify both. This verse shows the great attraction of the people for both Rukmiṇī and Kṛṣṇa.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The two are most suitable for each other. The word eva should be understood for both parties. The reason is that he and she are flawless (anavadyātmā). They desired the marriage of the two, offering their unlimited piety with devotion.

    Important Words
    • acyutaḥ — the infallible, Kṛṣṇa
      Name of Kṛṣṇa: a- (not) + cyuta (fallen). 'He who never falls from His position.' Gauḍīyas glos it as Bhagavān's permanence — He cannot fall from svarūpa, dharma, or vow. The citizens' use of this name is theologically loaded: only the unfallen one can be a true pati.
    • su - caritam — pious work
      Compound: su (well) + carita (deeds). The citizens are willing to liquidate their accumulated puṇya for this one outcome. Gauḍīyas read this as a folk-form of the proper bhakti-attitude: every karma's true purpose is the satisfaction of Kṛṣṇa.
    • tri - loka - kṛt — the creator of the three worlds
      Compound: tri (three) + loka (world) + kṛt (maker). The Creator is identified with Kṛṣṇa-as-Acyuta. The Gauḍīya siddhānta is here in the citizens' mouths: the supreme creator and the bridegroom of Rukmiṇī are one Person.
    May Acyuta, the creator of the three worlds, be satisfied with whatever pious work we may have done and show His mercy by taking the hand of Vaidarbhī.
    Purport

    The devoted citizens of Vidarbha lovingly offered their entire stock of pious credit to Princess Rukmiṇī. They were very eager to see her marry Lord Kṛṣṇa.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    May Acyuta, the creator of the three worlds, be satisfied with whatever pious work we may have done and show His mercy by taking the hand of Vaidarbhī.
    Commentary

    Krsna is satisfied with whatever pious acts we have done. We have given these pious acts to her account so she can marry Krsna.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    May the creator of the three worlds, he who can do anything, and who is merciful by creating the words so that we can live, be satisfied with whatever pious acts we have done in previous lives. He is fixed in beauty and qualities (acyutaḥ). They use the word vaidarbhyāḥ (she who is from Vidarbha) to indicate that they as residents of Vidarbha have a relationship with her. Because their hearts are overcome with the sweetness of Kṛṣṇa’s human pastimes, they use differing words to describe him (tri-loka-kṛt and acyutaḥ). They also indicate his extraordinary nature.

    Important Words
    • prema - kalā - baddhāḥ — bound by the increase of pure love
      Compound: prema (pure love) + kalā (portion, growing-phase, also 'art') + baddha (bound). The word prema is the technical highest stage of bhakti in Gauḍīya theology (Bhakti-rasāmṛta-sindhu 1.4). Vyāsa names the citizens' affection prema-kalā — Bhagavān's nearness produces it spontaneously.
    • ambikā - ālayam — the temple of Goddess Ambikā
      Compound: Ambikā (Pārvatī as 'Mother') + ālaya (abode). Ambikā in Gauḍīya theology is a Vaiṣṇavī devī — her temples are not rivals to Vaiṣṇavism but stations within it. Rukmiṇī's prayer in verse 46 will confirm this.
    • bhaṭaiḥ guptā — protected by guards
      Compound: bhaṭa (guard, soldier) + gupta (protected). The same root gup as in goptṛtve varaṇam (the fourth limb of śaraṇāgati). Outwardly the guards protect; inwardly Rukmiṇī has already chosen Kṛṣṇa as goptā.
    Bound by their swelling love, the city’s residents spoke in this way. Then the bride, protected by guards, left the inner palace to visit the temple of Ambikā.
    Purport

    Śrīla Viśvanātha Cakravartī quotes the Medinī dictionary’s definition of the word kalā as follows: kalā mūle pravṛddhau syāc chilādāv aṁśa-mātrake. “The word kalā means ‘a root,’ ‘increase,’ ‘a stone’ or ‘a mere part.’”

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Bound by their swelling love, the city's residents spoke in this way. Then the bride, protected by guards, left the inner palace to visit the temple of Ambikā.
    Commentary

    Under the influence of increased (kala) prema concerning Rukmini they spoke.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The residents spoke among themselves continually in this manner. They were not afraid of Rukmī because they were bound by effects of prema. Kalā means “producing.” Or they were bound by a particle (kalā) of prema which was pleasing to them. That prema was suitable for friendly emotions to the Lord and was exalted. They were bound up tightly by that particle of love. What then to speak of Rukmiṇī and other women? The word ca indicates that Rukmiṇī was aware of what the people spoke. Just as they had prema for her, she experienced prema for them. She also took their speech as an auspicious sign and therefore in joy entered (pra agāt) the Durgā temple.

    Important Words
    • mukunda - caraṇa - ambujam — the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa
      Compound: Mukunda (giver of liberation) + caraṇa (foot) + ambuja (lotus). The threefold name-of-feet is the central object of Gauḍīya meditation. Rūpa Gosvāmī's Stava-mālā repeats this exact image.
    • anudhyāyatī samyak — totally meditating
      Present participle of anu-√dhyai + adverb samyak (completely). Dhyāna is the seventh limb of aṣṭāṅga-yoga and a major Gauḍīya limb of bhakti (smaraṇam, SB 7.5.23). Rukmiṇī performs dhyāna while walking — sādhana inside daily life.
    • yata - vāk — maintaining silence
      Compound: yata (controlled) + vāk (speech). Mauna-vrata. Gauḍīyas distinguish empty silence (śūnya-mauna) from kṛṣṇa-smaraṇa-mauna; Rukmiṇī's silence is the latter — speech is restrained so that smaraṇa can flow.
    • padbhyām viniryayau — went out on foot
      Instrumental dual + perfect verb. She walks to the temple, not in a palanquin — Gauḍīyas read this as the bhakta's humility before the deity: the legs themselves become offerings.
    Rukmiṇī silently went out on foot to see the lotus feet of the deity Bhavānī. Accompanied by her mothers and girlfriends and protected by the King’s valiant soldiers, who held their upraised weapons at the ready, she simply absorbed her mind in the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa. And all the while mṛdaṅgas, conchshells, paṇavas, horns and other instruments resounded.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Rukmiṇī silently went out on foot to see the lotus feet of the deity Bhavānī. Accompanied by her mothers and girlfriends and protected by the King's valiant soldiers, who held their upraised weapons at the ready, she simply absorbed her mind in the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa. And all the while mṛdaṅgas, conchshells, paṇavas, horns and other instruments resounded.
    Commentary

    From the city up to the temple complex of Durga, she was protected in a palanquin .She then went four of five prakosthas (fifteen feet) out side the palanquin into the temple, while the guards stood outside in all directions. Mrdanga and conches began to sound.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The details are described in four verses. She (sāḥ), who was endowed with such greatness, went on foot, out of respect, because she was going to see Durgā’ lotus feet. Durgā’s feet are described as lotuses because of the Rukmiṇī’s devotion. “If Rukmiṇī is directly Lakṣmī, why does she have devotion to Durgā?” She was constantly meditating on the lotus feet of Mukunda, endowed completely (samyak) with sweetness, which revealed their softness and other qualities (like jasmine flowers). This indicates that neither she or Kṛṣṇa revealed their greatness at this time. Because she was absorbed in devotion, she was silent. She also walked with devotion (vi—niryayau). Being surrounded by many people indicates that she would be hard to steal and was thus in great anxiety. This shows the seed of experiencing joy on suddenly attaining Kṛṣṇa, which is described later. She was surrounded by persons who had motherly affection (mātṛbhiḥ). She was surrounded by troops because Rukmī was afraid of Kṛṣṇa. They were brave, dressed in armor, and had their weapons raised. These were progressively better means of protecting her. Mṛdaṅgas, paṇavas, and tūryas are drums. Bherīs are wind instruments. Another type of bherī is a drum.

    Personal Guidance
    Rukmiṇī silently walks on foot to Bhavānī's temple — accompanied by mothers, girlfriends, soldiers with raised weapons — simply absorbing her mind in Kṛṣṇa's feet. Silent, supported procession with focused mind is the bride's actual offering.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where in your processions do you fill space with chatter when silent absorption is the worship?
    • Who walks with you with 'raised weapons' on your devotional path?
    Analogy

    She walks to one temple but her mind walks to the other. Body in the Ambikā procession, mind on Mukunda's feet — the perfect picture of yukta-vairāgya: outer form preserved, inner attention undivided. This is exactly Rūpa Gosvāmī's prescription in Bhakti-rasāmṛta-sindhu: do the world's duties while the heart is fixed elsewhere.

    Stories
    Mīrā walking through Mewar's court

    Mīrābāī continued to attend the court of Mewar — to receive her brother-in-law, to follow protocol, to wear the queen's clothes — while her heart sang only kṛṣṇa-nāma. Outwardly the queen of Mewar; inwardly the bride of Giridhara.

    Gauḍīyas read SB 10.53.40 as the prototype: Rukmiṇī walks to Ambikā with her mothers and guards, but mukunda-caraṇa-ambujam is what she actually approaches. Mīrā is her direct lineage.

    Important Words
    • dvija - patnyaḥ — wives of brāhmaṇas
      Compound: dvija (twice-born) + patnī (wife). Brāhmaṇī-saṅga is treated by Gauḍīyas as sādhu-saṅga in adjacent form. Their songs and prayers along the route literally form a kīrtana procession around Rukmiṇī.
    • gāyantyaḥ — singing and offering prayers
      Two present participles. Gāna (singing) and stuti (prayer) are two of the nine limbs of bhakti — kīrtana proper. The wedding procession has, without anyone designing it, become a saṅkīrtana-yātrā.
    • sūta - māgadha - vandinaḥ — bards, chroniclers, heralds
      Triple compound. These are the lineage-singers of royal courts. Gauḍīyas note: the same office Sūta Gosvāmī fills in the SB itself. Even the structure of the procession mirrors the structure of the Bhāgavata's narration.
    Behind the bride followed thousands of prominent courtesans bearing various offerings and presents, along with well-adorned brāhmaṇas’ wives singing and reciting prayers and bearing gifts of garlands, scents, clothing and jewelry. There were also professional singers, musicians, bards, chroniclers and heralds.
    Purport

    Śrīla Viśvanātha Cakravartī explains that from her own quarters up to the temple of Bhavānī, Rukmiṇī went by palanquin and thus was easily protected. Only for the last twelve to fifteen feet, from the palace to the temple area, did she go on foot, with royal bodyguards stationed outside the temple on all sides.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Behind the bride followed thousands of prominent courtesans bearing various offerings and presents, along with well-adorned brāhmaṇas' wives singing and reciting prayers and bearing gifts of garlands, scents, clothing and jewelry. There were also professional singers, musicians, bards, chroniclers and heralds.
    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The best citizens came with various gifts and articles of worship (balibhiḥ). The singers sang and the sūtas and others praised (stuvantaḥ). The musicians played instruments (understood but not written in the text).

    Personal Guidance
    Behind her, thousands of courtesans bear offerings; brāhmaṇa wives sing, recite, bear garlands, scents, clothing, jewelry. Public ritual is layered with women's labor; female ritual work surrounds the bride.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where do you under-honor women's ritual work in your own community?
    • What contribution from women might be invisibly carrying your devotional life?
    Analogy

    A river of music, garlands and women flows behind her — and at the head of the river, one girl walking silent. The procession's noise is the world's; her silence is bhakti's. Gauḍīyas savor the contrast: the louder the sa-puruṣa world around the devotee, the quieter the inner kṛṣṇa-smaraṇa.

    Important Words
    • upaspṛśya — sipping water for purification
      Absolutive of upa-√spṛś (to touch lightly, perform ācamana). The standard pre-pūjā ritual. Gauḍīyas note: Rukmiṇī performs the very acts she will later perform countless times as a queen of Dvārakā in front of Kṛṣṇa's deity.
    • śuciḥ śāntā — sanctified and peaceful
      Two predicate adjectives. Śuci (pure) + śāntā (peaceful). Śānta is the first of the five rasas in Rūpa's enumeration. Rukmiṇī enters Ambikā's temple in the lowest rasa-key and will exit, on Kṛṣṇa's chariot, in mādhurya — the whole ladder of rasa is climbed in one chapter.
    • ambikā - antikam — the presence of Ambikā
      Compound: Ambikā + antika (near). Antika emphasizes proximity, not just location — Rukmiṇī comes near to the goddess in the sense of being granted access. Gauḍīyas treat the moment as devī's hospitality to the future Lakṣmī.
    Upon reaching the goddess’s temple, Rukmiṇī first washed her lotus feet and hands and then sipped water for purification. Thus sanctified and peaceful, she came into the presence of mother Ambikā.
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    Upon reaching the goddess's temple, Rukmiṇī first washed her lotus feet and hands and then sipped water for purification. Thus sanctified and peaceful, she came into the presence of mother Ambikā.
    Commentary

    Rukmini, performing acamana (upasprsya), entered the inner sanctum (devi or deva sadanam). The masculine is sometimes used for female deities in their sanctum just as the masculine is used for female animals while they are in the egg or womb.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Six verses describe Rukmiṇī’s devotion to Durgā. She arrived at Durgā’s temple (deva-sadanam). The masculine deva is used since Śiva and others were also situated in the temple or since the masculine is used for words like “eggs” of the hen even though so many of the eggs may be female chicks. Her mind was controlled (śāntāḥ).

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    She reached the temple of Durgā (deva-sadanam). Another version has devyāḥ. Śāntāḥ means her mind was controlled.

    Personal Guidance
    Reaching the temple, Rukmiṇī washes feet and hands, sips water for purification; sanctified and peaceful, she enters Ambikā's presence. Multiple purifications precede entry; the temple receives the already-prepared.
    Reflection Questions
    • Where do you enter sacred spaces unprepared and wonder why nothing lands?
    • What multi-step purification could you actually perform?
    Analogy

    Before entering the deity's presence she washes her lotus hands with water — clean, calm, vow of silence intact. The verse is a compressed image of arcana-vidhi: ācamana, śuddhi, śāntā-bhāva, then darśana. Rukmiṇī is a model arcaka before she becomes a bride.

    Important Words
    • pravayasaḥ — elderly wives of brāhmaṇas
      Compound: pravayas (advanced in age) + vipra (brāhmaṇa) + yoṣit (woman). Senior brāhmaṇa-wives are the proper guides for a young bride's first arcana. Gauḍīyas read this as the female lineage of śikṣā-paramparā — sevā taught by elders to juniors.
    • bhava - patnīm bhava - anvitām — wife of Bhava, accompanied by Bhava
      Compound twice repeated: Bhava (Śiva) + patnī (wife) + anvitā (accompanied by). The verse names Pārvatī through her relation to Bhava. Gauḍīyas note: śakti is always related, never absolute; Ambikā derives her function from Bhava, as Bhava derives his from Viṣṇu (śiva-virañci-nutam).
    • vandayām cakruḥ — they led her in offering respects
      Periphrastic perfect causative of √vand. Vandanam — one of the nine limbs of bhakti. The verb is causative (they made her vandana) because bhakti is transmitted through living teachers' hands.
    The older wives of brāhmaṇas, expert in the knowledge of rituals, led young Rukmiṇī in offering respects to Bhavānī, who appeared with her consort, Lord Bhava.
    Purport

    According to the ācāryas, here the term bhavānvitām indicates that in the Ambikā temple visited by Rukmiṇī, the presiding deity was the goddess, whose husband appeared in an accompanying role. Thus the ritual was properly performed by women. Śrīla Viśvanātha Cakravartī comments that the term vidhi-jñāḥ may be understood to mean that since the learned wives of brāhmaṇas knew of Rukmiṇī’s desire to marry Kṛṣṇa, the verb vandayāṁ cakruḥ thus indicates that they prompted her to pray for what she really wanted. In this way, like the goddess Bhavānī, Rukmiṇī could be united with her eternal male companion.

    — A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    The older wives of brāhmaṇas, expert in the knowledge of rituals, led young Rukmiṇī in offering respects to Bhavānī, who appeared with her consort, Lord Bhava.
    Commentary

    The aged wives of the priests, knowing the rule of scripture and also the mind of Rukmini, had her worship Durga along with Siva. "O Durga, just you are the wife of Siva, and joined with him, make Rukmini the wife of Krsna, joined with him." Having seen Krsna, they prayed in the same way as the citizens had previously, "May our pious acts be given to her."

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    The words bhavānīm and bhava-patnīm indicate that Durgā was Śiva’s assistant in fulfilling desires (bhava= worldly desires) and in fulfilling dharma (bhava= excellence). In fulfilling desires, she arranges for women to marry men. In relation to fulfilling dharma she helps in sacrifices. The words show her intimate relationship with the great devotee Śiva. Rukmiṇī was made to offer respects to chaste Durgā, associated with Śiva. The elderly women also taught her the mantra in the next verse. They had realized the mantra.

    Śrīdhara Svāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    Bhāvānī refers to Pārvatī. They had Ṛukmiṇi offer respects to bhava-patnim (wife of Śiva) with devotion (bhavānvitam). By offering respects to her, offering respects to Śiva was also accomplished. Or she worshipped her in order to gain similar chastity and good fortune.

    Important Words
    • namasye — I offer my obeisances
      First-person middle present of √nam, expressing devotion to the self's benefit. The classical opening word of stuti and stotra literature. Gauḍīyas pair this verb with the namaḥ of the praṇava — pure vandanam, the second limb of bhakti.
    • ambike — O Ambikā
      Vocative. Ambikā ('Mother') is the maternal form of Pārvatī. Gauḍīyas note: she is addressed as a mother — the bride does not flatter her as queen but appeals to her as mother to a daughter; bhakti's relational vocabulary is always specific.
    • śivām — the wife of Lord Śiva (also: the auspicious one)
      Accusative of Śivā. Pun: Śivā as wife of Śiva, also as 'auspicious.' Gauḍīyas read the pun as the Vaiṣṇava attitude: the truly śivā-auspicious is the one whose puṣṭi gives Kṛṣṇa.
    • bhūyāt patiḥ me bhagavān kṛṣṇaḥ — may Lord Kṛṣṇa become my husband
      Optative + nominative + nominative + nominative. The actual prayer. Gauḍīyas treat this short line as a model śaraṇāgati-mantra: every other element is preamble, this is the iṣṭa. Patiḥ here is both husband and Lord — the Vaiṣṇava ślesa.
    • tat anumodatām — please allow that
      Demonstrative + imperative of anu-√mud. Anumodana is a precise theological term — sanctioning, blessing-by-rejoicing. Ambikā is asked not to grant but to anumodana, to bless what Bhagavān has already decided. Gauḍīyas read this as deep deva-tattva: the devas anumodana what Viṣṇu wills.
    [Princess Rukmiṇī prayed:] O mother Ambikā, wife of Lord Siva, I repeatedly offer my obeisances unto you, together with your children. May Lord Kṛṣṇa become my husband. Please grant this!
    Gauḍīya Ācāryas
    Viśvanātha Cakravartī Ṭhākura Gauḍīya
    Translation
    [Princess Rukmiṇī prayed:] O mother Ambikā, wife of Lord Siva, I repeatedly offer my obeisances unto you, together with your children. May Lord Kṛṣṇa become my husband. Please grant this!
    Commentary

    They had her chant the mantra mentioned in this verse. "May Ganesa remove all the obstacles I have now before me. May Krsna be my husband. May you approve it." "So be it. May he be your husband," answered Durga.

    Jīva Gosvāmī Gauḍīya
    Commentary

    This verse is the mantra for offering respects to Durgā. O mother of the universe (ambike)! She is -called Śivā since she is non-different from Śiva, having similar qualities and name. Therefore she offers respects to Durgā along with Śiva. After indicating Durgā’s qualification of being like Śiva, she makes her request. May the Lord who is endowed with all unparalleled sweetness and powers (bhagavān) and who attracts the minds of everyone (kṛṣṇaḥ), what to speak of those who are dedicated to him, be my husband. You two should permit this since you can fulfill desires. Or, may Kṛṣṇa permit it. In great longing, she forgets about Durgā.
